z-m-33-01.title: Given three points, is the remaining point just one?
z-m-33-01.topic: Finding the remaining vertex of a parallelogram when three vertices are given
z-m-33-01.goal: Judge whether the remaining vertex of a parallelogram is fixed to one point when only three vertices are known, say why it is not fixed and what further information is needed (the order of the vertex names), and find the possible points yourself.
z-m-33-01.material: On a coordinate plane there are three points A(0, 0), B(4, 1), C(5, 4). How to read them: A is 'zero, zero', B is 'four, one', C is 'five, four'. These three points are not on one line. You want to choose a point D so that the four points A, B, C, D are the vertices of one parallelogram. The original problem only says 'let the fourth vertex be D', and it does not say in what order the vertices are connected. All coordinates are real numbers, and the four points are different from each other.
z-m-33-01.thinking.0: Judging whether the information is enough
z-m-33-01.thinking.1: Splitting the possible cases and finding them without missing any
z-m-33-01.thinking.2: Explaining how extra information reduces the number of cases
z-m-33-01.prereq.0: Plotting points on a coordinate plane and reading the direction and amount of movement between two points
z-m-33-01.prereq.1: Properties of a parallelogram (opposite sides are parallel and equal in length, the diagonals bisect each other) - middle school level
z-m-33-01.prereq.2: (This is a task placed at H2 for production convenience; it indicates a difficulty level, not a grade placement. It is assumed to be taught after 'plane coordinates' in Common Mathematics.)
z-m-33-01.s.s1.prompt: Is the position of point D fixed by the information above? Choose the most suitable judgment.
z-m-33-01.s.s1.hint.0: Plot A, B, and C on a coordinate plane and add one more point to these three to make a parallelogram.
z-m-33-01.s.s1.hint.1: Change which of the three points is opposite D, plot D each time, and check by eye each time whether the opposite sides are parallel.
z-m-33-01.s.s1.o.a: It is fixed to one. The three points are fixed, so the last point is only one too
z-m-33-01.s.s1.r.a: You assumed that once three points are fixed, the rest is fixed to one. Remember that the name of a quadrilateral (ABCD) has an order built into it.
z-m-33-01.s.s1.o.b: It is not fixed. Sides only need to be parallel, so there are infinitely many
z-m-33-01.s.s1.r.b: It seems you read the parallel condition as only one pair. A parallelogram has both pairs of sides parallel, and two more conditions fix a point. Plot points yourself to check.
z-m-33-01.s.s1.o.c: It is not fixed. It depends on which point is made opposite which
z-m-33-01.s.s1.r.c: You pointed out that D changes when the opposite pair changes. If you also count how many possible pairs there are, you will see the number.
z-m-33-01.s.s1.o.d: It is not fixed. There are 2 possible points
z-m-33-01.s.s1.r.d: You saw that there are several D, but it seems you counted only some of them. Go through every point that could be opposite D, one at a time.
z-m-33-01.s.s1.explain: Depending on which of the three points A, B, C is opposite D, the parallelogram changes, so there are three possible places for D. If you are given the information that the vertex names are connected in order (for example, quadrilateral ABCD), the opposite pairs are fixed and D narrows to one. So the extra information needed in this problem is the order of the vertices.
z-m-33-01.s.s2.prompt: Find and enter 3 different points D(x, y) that meet the condition. It is enough that the four points are vertices of one parallelogram in some order. In the box below, first write only the coordinates of the points, and then write the reasons.
z-m-33-01.s.s2.hint.0: Choose one of the three points and call it 'opposite D', then look at how D is related to the segment joining the other two points.
z-m-33-01.s.s2.hint.1: Change the point you choose as the opposite one in the order A, B, C, and compare whether the resulting D are different from each other.
z-m-33-01.s.s2.ok.c1: This is a position where A, B, C, D become vertices of one parallelogram.
z-m-33-01.s.s2.fail.c1: With this point D, connecting A, B, C, D in any order does not make a parallelogram. Check whether the midpoints of the two opposite points are the same.
z-m-33-01.s.s2.explain: The possible D are the three points (9, 5), (1, 3), (-1, -3). They are the cases where D is opposite A, B, and C respectively, and in each case the midpoints of the two opposite points are at the same position.
z-m-33-01.s.s2.because.prompt: Write why D is not fixed to one, and what you think about whether there could be more possible D.
z-m-33-01.s.s2.because.hint.0: Mark which of A, B, C each point you plotted is opposite to.
z-m-33-01.s.s2.because.hint.1: Count how many points can be opposite D.
z-m-33-01.s.s2.because.selfAssess.0: Did I explain why D changes as 'which point it is opposite to'?
z-m-33-01.s.s2.because.selfAssess.1: Did I write, even in one line, a reason for 'could there be more' (the evidence that I split all the cases)?
z-m-33-01.s.s2.because.selfAssess.2: Did I pick one point I plotted and check again whether its opposite sides are parallel?
z-m-33-01.s.s2.because.model.0: D changes depending on which two points you take as opposite vertices. If it is opposite A it is (9, 5), if opposite B it is (1, 3), and if opposite C it is (-1, -3). Only A, B, C can be opposite D, so 3 is all there is.
z-m-33-01.s.s2.because.model.1: The midpoints of the diagonals have to be the same, so choosing one of the three points as the one opposite D gives one D each. There are 3 ways to choose, so D has 3 places, and I think there can't be more.
z-m-33-01.s.s2.because.modelNote.1: Even if you didn't write the coordinates, it is enough if you have the number and the reason.
z-m-33-01.s.s3.prompt: New information has arrived. When you checked the problem again, it said 'parallelogram ABCD', and the vertices are connected in the order A, B, C, D (A and C are opposite, B and D are opposite). Where is D now?
z-m-33-01.s.s3.hint.0: Write down which vertices are next to D in ABCD.
z-m-33-01.s.s3.hint.1: Pick a point and check yourself whether the move from side AB to side DC has the same direction and the same size.
z-m-33-01.s.s3.r.a: You read it as A and D being opposite. In the order ABCD, the opposite pairs are A and C, and B and D.
z-m-33-01.s.s3.r.b: You placed it so that B and D are opposite. Check whether the opposite sides AB and DC have the same direction and length.
z-m-33-01.s.s3.r.c: You read it as C and D being opposite. In the order ABCD, the neighbors of C are B and D.
z-m-33-01.s.s3.o.d: It still can't be known which of the three places it is
z-m-33-01.s.s3.r.d: You missed that the order fixes the opposite pairs. Once the order is given, write down which point is opposite A and which is opposite B.
z-m-33-01.s.s3.explain: In the order ABCD, B and D are opposite, so D = A + C - B, that is, (0+5-4, 0+4-1) = (1, 3). Check: vector AB = (4, 1), and vector DC = (5-1, 4-3) = (4, 1), which is the same. The new information narrowed it down to one of the three possible places.

z-m-33-02.title: If a line comes out, do the two circles meet?
z-m-33-02.topic: The position of two circles and the line that comes from the equations of the two circles
z-m-33-02.goal: Use examples to check that even if a line always comes out of the equations of two circles, that alone does not mean the circles meet, and build two circles that do not meet yourself to say what else needs to be checked.
z-m-33-02.material: The equation of circle C1 is x²+y²=4 (center (0, 0), radius 2). How to read it: 'x squared plus y squared equals 4'. Circle C2 has center (d, 0) and radius r, with d>0, r>0. Its equation is (x-d)²+y²=r². Hayun subtracted the equation of C2 from the equation of C1 side by side to get a first-degree expression in x, and said, 'A line came out, so the two circles meet at the two points this line passes through.' Here, two circles 'meet' means there is a point that lies on both circles (including the case where they touch).
z-m-33-02.thinking.0: Distinguishing the conditions where the claim holds from examples where it does not
z-m-33-02.thinking.1: Revising your judgment and confidence as new information arrives
z-m-33-02.thinking.2: Building counterexamples yourself and sorting them into kinds
z-m-33-02.prereq.0: The meaning of the circle equation (x-a)²+(y-b)²=r² and reading the center and radius
z-m-33-02.prereq.1: The meaning of the positions of two circles (apart, touching, meeting at two points, one containing the other)
z-m-33-02.prereq.2: (This is a task placed at H2 for production convenience; it indicates a difficulty level, not a grade placement. It is assumed to come after learning the equation of a circle in Common Mathematics.)
z-m-33-02.s.s1.prompt: The data will be revealed one at a time. Each time, judge at how many points the two circles meet, and think about how far you can trust Hayun's statement.
z-m-33-02.s.s1.hint.1: When d and r change, compare the distance between the two centers with the sum of the radii.
z-m-33-02.s.s1.st.0.info: Subtracting the equations of C1 and C2 gives 2dx = d² + 4 - r², so as long as d is not 0, you get a line where x is a single value. The values of d and r are not known yet.
z-m-33-02.s.s1.st.0.ask: Can you say 'the two circles meet' just from the fact that a line came out?
z-m-33-02.s.s1.st.0.after: A line coming out is the information that 'if there are intersection points, they lie on this line'. The guarantee that there are intersection points must be checked separately. Let's test it with the next data.
z-m-33-02.s.s1.st.0.o.a: You can say so. Every common point of the two circles lies on this line
z-m-33-02.s.s1.st.0.r.a: It seems you read 'if there is a common point, it lies on the line' as 'there is a common point'. The first statement is about when a point exists.
z-m-33-02.s.s1.st.0.o.b: You can't say so. All you can know is that if there are meeting points, they lie on this line
z-m-33-02.s.s1.st.0.r.b: You separated what the line tells you from what it does not tell you.
z-m-33-02.s.s1.st.0.o.c: You can't say so. A line coming out actually means the two circles do not meet
z-m-33-02.s.s1.st.0.r.c: You read the fact that a line came out as evidence in the opposite direction. Think about whether a line also comes out for two circles that do meet.
z-m-33-02.s.s1.st.0.o.d: If you don't know the values of d and r, this line tells you nothing
z-m-33-02.s.s1.st.0.r.d: Without the values you cannot know whether there are intersection points, but you can say where they would be if there are. Check whether this line really gives no information.
z-m-33-02.s.s1.st.1.info: It is fixed that d = 6, r = 1. Subtracting the equations gives 12x = 39, that is, the line x = 13/4 = 3.25. For a point on this line to also lie on C1, you need y² = 4 - (13/4)² = -105/16 (y is real).
z-m-33-02.s.s1.st.1.ask: At how many points do the two circles meet?
z-m-33-02.s.s1.st.1.after: y² is negative, so there is no point of C1 on this line. This also fits the fact that the distance 6 between the centers is greater than the sum of the radii, 3, so the circles are apart. A line came out, but the two circles do not meet. The fact that a line always comes out is not evidence of intersection points.
z-m-33-02.s.s1.st.1.o.a: 2 points. As Hayun said, a line came out, so they meet at two points
z-m-33-02.s.s1.st.1.r.a: You keep accepting the line coming out as evidence of intersection points. Look at whether there really is a point of C1 on this line.
z-m-33-02.s.s1.st.1.o.b: 1 point. The line and C1 meet at one point
z-m-33-02.s.s1.st.1.r.b: You thought of the case where a line and a circle meet, but it seems you did not check the sign of y². When y² is negative, is there a real y?
z-m-33-02.s.s1.st.1.o.c: 0 points. There is no point of C1 on the line
z-m-33-02.s.s1.st.1.r.c: You judged based on the result of matching the points on the line with the equation of C1.
z-m-33-02.s.s1.st.2.info: You changed to d = 3, r = 2. Subtracting the equations gives 6x = 9, that is, the line x = 3/2. Putting it into C1 gives y² = 4 - 9/4 = 7/4.
z-m-33-02.s.s1.st.2.ask: This time, at how many points do the two circles meet?
z-m-33-02.s.s1.st.2.after: y = ±√7/2 (about ±1.32), so they meet at the two points (3/2, ±√7/2). It also works on the C2 side: (3/2 - 3)² + 7/4 = 4. In this case Hayun's conclusion was right. What decides whether they meet is not the fact that a line came out, but whether there are points of C1 on that line.
z-m-33-02.s.s1.st.2.o.a: 2 points. y takes two values, positive and negative, so there are two points
z-m-33-02.s.s1.st.2.r.a: You read that y takes two values from y² = 7/4.
z-m-33-02.s.s1.st.2.o.b: 0 points. Even though a line came out, as last time, they do not meet
z-m-33-02.s.s1.st.2.r.b: You applied the earlier example as it was to this one. Compare whether the sign of y² this time is the same as before.
z-m-33-02.s.s1.st.2.o.c: 1 point. There is only one point of C1 on the line
z-m-33-02.s.s1.st.2.r.c: Count how many y come from a single value of y². If y² is positive, how many y are there?
z-m-33-02.s.s1.st.3.info: You changed to d = 4, r = 2. Subtracting the equations gives 8x = 16, that is, the line x = 2. Putting it into C1 gives y² = 4 - 4 = 0.
z-m-33-02.s.s1.st.3.ask: At how many points do the two circles meet?
z-m-33-02.s.s1.st.3.after: There is only y = 0, so they touch at the one point (2, 0). This is the case where the distance 4 between the centers equals the sum of the radii 2+2. In this case the line x = 2 is the common tangent of the two circles. Even when a line comes out, the number of intersection points can be 0, 1, or 2.
z-m-33-02.s.s1.st.3.o.a: 0 points. A line came out, but it does not meet C1
z-m-33-02.s.s1.st.3.r.a: You may have read y² = 0 as 'no solution'. Check whether there is a real y that satisfies y² = 0.
z-m-33-02.s.s1.st.3.o.b: 1 point. There is only one point of C1 on the line
z-m-33-02.s.s1.st.3.r.b: You saw that if y² = 0, there is only one y.
z-m-33-02.s.s1.st.3.o.c: 2 points. As in the earlier step, the line passes through two points
z-m-33-02.s.s1.st.3.r.c: You carried over the result of the earlier step as it was. Compare how many y come from the y² value this time with how many came earlier.
z-m-33-02.s.s1.reflect: How did your belief about the fact that a line came out change as you went through the examples? What was different between the cases where Hayun's statement was right and the cases where it was wrong? What must you always check after a line comes out?
z-m-33-02.s.s2.prompt: Make examples yourself where Hayun's statement is wrong. Choose the center (d, 0) and radius r of C2 and enter 2 different kinds of cases where the two circles do not meet. Let one example be where the two circles are apart outside each other, and the other where one circle contains the other so they do not meet.
z-m-33-02.s.s2.hint.0: Compare the radius 2 of C1 with r and think about how large the distance d between the centers must be for them to be apart.
z-m-33-02.s.s2.hint.1: To put one circle inside the other, try out how to choose d by comparing it with the difference of the radii.
z-m-33-02.s.s2.hint.2: After choosing candidates, compare them with the example you saw earlier, such as d = 6, r = 1, and check that they are of the same kind.
z-m-33-02.s.s2.var.d: x-coordinate d of the center of C2
z-m-33-02.s.s2.ok.c1: Both d and r are positive.
z-m-33-02.s.s2.fail.c1: Both d and r must be greater than 0.
z-m-33-02.s.s2.ok.c2: The two circles do not meet.
z-m-33-02.s.s2.fail.c2: These two circles meet or touch. It has to be an example where they do not meet. Compare the distance between the centers with the radii.
z-m-33-02.s.s2.explain: Example: (d, r) = (5, 1) has distance between centers 5, greater than the sum of the radii 3, so they are apart outside, and (1, 5) has C2 containing C1, so they do not meet (the radius of C1 is 2, and the center distance 1 is less than the difference of the two radii, 3). In both cases d > 0, so a line comes out, but the two circles do not meet. A case of touching from the inside (for example, d = 2, r = 4) meets at one point, so it doesn't count.
z-m-33-02.s.s3.prompt: Tell Hayun: when you subtract the equations and a line comes out, what else must be checked before you can say 'the two circles meet', and why? Write it.
z-m-33-02.s.s3.hint.0: First write in one line why, in the example d = 6, r = 1, they did not meet even though a line came out.
z-m-33-02.s.s3.hint.1: Recall by what calculation or comparison you learned in that example that they do not meet.
z-m-33-02.s.s3.placeholder: Example: Even if a line comes out, ...
z-m-33-02.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did I distinguish, in my own words, that the fact that a line came out and the fact that the two circles meet are not the same thing?
z-m-33-02.s.s3.selfAssess.1: If I apply the checking method I wrote to the example d = 6, r = 1, does it give the conclusion that they do not meet?
z-m-33-02.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did I say when the points the line passes through lie on both circles?
z-m-33-02.s.s3.model.0: Even if a line comes out, you have to check separately whether there is a common point of the two circles on that line. Put the line into the equation of one circle and see whether a real intersection point comes out, and if not, the two circles do not meet.
z-m-33-02.s.s3.model.1: You can also compare the distance between the centers with the sum or difference of the radii. A line always comes out unless d is 0, so just having a line does not guarantee intersection points, and you have to check whether there really are intersection points.
z-m-33-02.s.s3.modelNote.1: Both the method of substituting into the line and the method of comparing distances are accepted.
z-m-33-02.s.s1.hint.0: Substitute the coordinates of a point on the line directly into the equation of C1 to check whether it really satisfies it too.
z-m-33-02.s.s3.model.2: You have to compare the distance d between the centers of the two circles with the sum of the radii 2+r and the difference |2-r|. If it is greater than the sum or less than the difference, the two circles do not meet even if a line comes out.
z-m-33-02.s.s3.modelNote.2: An answer using distance comparison is also accepted.
